segments.title: Reading a treaty through its delegates
segments.body: A government's choice of delegates can reveal priorities that its stated objectives leave unclear. The Dutch 1913-14 battleship tender provides the comparison: British and German yards answered the same requirement with different emphases on capabilities and secondary missions. Signatory delegates could shape negotiations, report back to their governments, and decide whether to put their names to the result. Other specialists could advise them, but could not commit a state in the same way. The delegates' responsibilities and experience therefore help explain the choices made during a conference.

evidence.note: Governments' choice of signatories helps reveal their priorities, since those delegates had special influence over the treaty.

segments.summary: Who each government sent to Washington reveals its priorities and whether the resulting treaty could win support at home.

segments.title: American citizens and the authority to sign a treaty
segments.body: The American signatories were styled as citizens of the United States, while other delegations carried ranks and titles. That wording distinguished the republic from states with systems of knighthoods and nobility. An ordinary citizen could not commit the country to a treaty simply by signing it. The chosen representatives still exercised official authority, whatever form their description took.

evidence.note: The American signatories' description as citizens contrasted with other delegations' titles, while their power to commit a state depended on official authority.

segments.summary: Calling the American delegates citizens expressed a republican identity while leaving their official treaty-making authority intact.

segments.title: American status, spending, and Senate ratification
segments.body: Secretary of State Charles Evans Hughes represented the administration, while Henry Cabot Lodge and Oscar Underwood brought the Senate majority and minority leadership into the negotiations. Elihu Root supplied a public rationale centred on peace and disarmament. The United States sought recognition of parity with Britain while avoiding the cost of an unchecked naval contest, particularly where Japanese construction could prompt further American building. Including both Senate leaders connected the international negotiations to the domestic approval process. Hughes could present the government's case with the people needed to carry the result through the Senate already involved.

evidence.note: Hughes, Lodge, Underwood, and Root brought executive authority, Senate leadership, and peace advocacy to the American delegation.
The American delegation sought global status and lower costs, relief from Japanese construction pressure, and a settlement structured to win Senate ratification.

segments.summary: The American delegation sought global recognition and a cheaper alternative to competing capital-ship programmes.

segments.title: British delegates and differing views on disarmament
segments.body: Britain's delegates brought experience in government, the Admiralty, and diplomacy. Arthur James Balfour was a former prime minister and Lord President of the Privy Council, while Lee was First Lord of the Admiralty. Auckland Campbell Geddes was the ambassador to the United States and, in this comparison, the delegate closest to supporting defence cuts. All represented Lloyd George's government, whose hopes for peace included general disarmament. That policy depended on other states agreeing to disarm as well.

evidence.note: Balfour, Lee, and Geddes held different offices and differed in sympathy toward defence cuts while representing Lloyd George's government.

segments.summary: Balfour, Lee, and Geddes brought different responsibilities and attitudes to a government pursuing peace through disarmament.

segments.title: New Zealand's naval protection and manpower limits
segments.body: New Zealand's representative, John William Salmond, was a judge and legal officer. The Dominion needed a strong Royal Navy for protection while having limited money to contribute to it. Providing crews presented a further constraint. HMS New Zealand illustrates the distinction between supporting a major ship and being able to sustain it through a separate local naval service.

evidence.note: Salmond's legal background, New Zealand's reliance on the Royal Navy, and the money and manpower constraints illustrated by HMS New Zealand.

segments.summary: New Zealand needed British naval protection while facing limits on both financial contributions and the crews it could provide.

segments.title: Industrial capacity behind American arms control
segments.body: Britain, the United States, Japan, and Italy competed over warship quality and technology, while German naval laws emphasized ship numbers for a risk-fleet strategy. Britain's industrial capabilities and export market rewarded continued technical competition. American political enthusiasm for continuous construction had weakened, yet the country's industrial base could still outproduce Japan. Japanese building was the immediate pressure that might prompt Congress to fund more ships. Limits on that construction offered Washington savings alongside recognition of parity with Britain. Formal equality in the treaty did not itself transfer global predominance to the United States; that shift is placed after the Second World War in this interpretation.

evidence.note: Qualitative naval competition, American capacity to outproduce Japan, and the savings and status sought through treaty limits. Formal parity is distinguished from the later transfer of global predominance.

segments.summary: American industrial capacity supported bargaining over naval limits, while restrictions on Japanese construction offered savings and recognition of parity with Britain.

segments.title: British disarmament ideals and imperial cruiser needs
segments.body: David Lloyd George hoped disarmament could reduce the chance of another continental catastrophe, while Britain still had to defend distant routes and possessions. Britain wanted two new battleships to replace older ships and resisted numerical cruiser limits. The imperial plan expected Dominion cruiser squadrons to patrol sea lanes and counter surface raiders, with destroyers and possibly submarines alongside them. The treaty limited cruiser size while leaving total numbers unrestricted, with the Hawkins class supplying the benchmark. Balfour's political connections, the First Lord's responsibility for obtaining the naval budget, and the ambassador's knowledge of American contacts brought different experience to the delegation. Britain's cruiser plans still depended on Dominion governments paying for forces that most did not build on the scale London envisaged.

evidence.note: British aims included two replacement battleships and unrestricted cruiser numbers for imperial defence. Dominion squadrons depended on local funding, while the delegation combined political, Admiralty, and diplomatic experience.

segments.summary: Britain entered seeking peace and economy, but would not accept limits that prevented it from policing a global empire with cruisers.

segments.title: Treaty limits and the problem of enforcement
segments.body: A hypothetical Italian cruiser built one thousand tons overweight raises the question of whether Britain or the United States would risk war to enforce a technical breach. Leaders would have to justify casualties and public expenditure over a displacement figure. An agreement without an impartial enforcement power depended on governments being willing to bear those costs. Its terms therefore had to give each participant a reason to comply in its own interest.

evidence.note: A cruiser exceeding its treaty displacement illustrates the enforcement problem.

segments.summary: Arms limits require more than signatures: governments must judge whether a violation is serious enough to enforce at real political cost.

segments.title: Dominion security depended on the Royal Navy
segments.body: Canada was willing to contribute money and supplies while avoiding the expense of a substantial peacetime fleet. Australia sought stronger local forces because maritime communications and widely separated population centres made sea power central to its security. New Zealand, with less population and fewer resources, depended even more directly on British naval strength. Those different circumstances still produced a united Commonwealth position against numerical cruiser limits because each Dominion relied on British ships to cover risks it could not meet alone.

evidence.note: The Dominions differed in resources and local forces but shared a reliance on the Royal Navy.

segments.summary: Canada, Australia, and New Zealand wanted different levels of local naval effort, but all had a stake in a strong Royal Navy.

segments.title: Canadian economy versus visible deterrence
segments.body: Theoretical mobilization capacity did not have the deterrent effect of visible warships already at sea. A hypothetical Canadian force of three Queen Elizabeth-class battleships illustrates the difference: opponents would have to reckon with those ships in peacetime, and Britain would gain their strength in war. Ottawa instead preferred financial and supply support while avoiding a substantial standing fleet. A cruiser squadron developed from 1911 offered another possible path for Canadian naval growth. The preference for economy left much of the peacetime naval burden with Britain.

evidence.note: A hypothetical Canadian force of three Queen Elizabeth-class battleships illustrates visible deterrence, alongside the alternative of cruiser development from 1911 and Canada's preference for money and supply contributions.

segments.summary: Canada could promise great wartime potential, but only ships already in service would create an immediate peacetime deterrent.

segments.title: Australian sea security and competitive shipbuilding
segments.body: Australia wanted to retain a capital ship as its flagship and to build up its own naval forces. Competition among multiple shipyards made large warships more affordable than a comparison with modern single-supplier carrier construction suggests. The sea formed Australia's defensive depth, while its widely separated population centres could not easily support one another. Maritime trade was also central to its economy. These conditions gave Australia a direct interest in both local naval strength and unrestricted cruiser numbers, and helped explain its support for Britain's negotiating position.

evidence.note: Competitive yard economics made major ships more attainable, while Australia's maritime geography and trade gave it a direct need for naval strength.

segments.summary: Australia's dispersed population and maritime trade made naval forces essential, while interwar yard competition made major ships more attainable than modern monopolies suggest.

segments.title: Royal dockyards, profit margins, and continuous work
segments.body: Public ownership is proposed as one response when a navy depends on a single company for carrier construction. Removing the private supplier's profit margin might reduce ship prices. A Royal dockyard would still need a continuous building programme, since the government would pay its workforce during gaps in orders. That obligation helps explain the preference for private yards despite their monopoly position.

evidence.note: The proposed return to Royal dockyards could remove private profit margins but would require continuous construction to keep the workforce employed.

segments.summary: A proposal to restore Royal dockyards weighs possible savings against the government's obligation to sustain construction between orders.

segments.title: Why one Commonwealth navy mattered to the ratios
segments.body: Separate Dominion allowances could have made a formal capital-ship ratio misleading. Britain plus individual allowances for Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, and India might have produced a much larger combined force than nominal Anglo-American parity suggested. Counting Commonwealth forces together closed that accounting route. It also bound Australia and New Zealand more tightly to the Royal Navy for security, showing how treaty ratios depended on constitutional definitions as much as ship totals.

evidence.note: Counting one Commonwealth navy shapes the proposed treatment of Dominion capital ships within treaty ratios.

segments.summary: Treating the Dominions as part of one naval establishment prevented British strength from being multiplied through nominally separate fleets.

segments.title: South Africa and the neglected Cape sea route
segments.body: Jan Smuts's choice of Balfour combined a gesture of imperial trust with distance from naval commitments. South Africa appeared remote from likely attackers, yet sat astride the diversion route that became vital whenever the Suez Canal or Mediterranean could not carry traffic. Protea, the navy's only Flower-class corvette, entered service after the Second World War. South African air patrols, trawlers, and other vessels nevertheless contributed during the war, when convoys passed the Cape to support North Africa and the Far East. The criticism concerns the limited investment in naval forces despite the route's importance, while acknowledging those wartime contributions.

evidence.note: South Africa's apparent remoteness and Smuts's selection of Balfour accompany a critique of naval investment. Protea's postwar service contrasts with wartime convoy needs, with maritime air patrols and auxiliary vessels acknowledged.

segments.summary: South Africa's sense of geographic safety obscured the naval importance of the Cape route and encouraged reliance on outside fleets.

segments.title: India's navy as security and nation-building
segments.body: India needed naval power for its long coastlines, trade, and central position in the Indian Ocean. A navy could also mix communities aboard ship and help develop institutions for an anticipated future nation-state. Regiments rooted in particular places could retain divisions that mixed ship crews brought into daily contact. Naval technical work offered capable people from lower and lower-middle-class backgrounds opportunities to rise within the service and society. Safe seamanship and machinery operation demanded competence regardless of noble birth. Indian political representatives and the Royal Navy could support expansion even when career administrators preferred to spend the money elsewhere. Naval development therefore depended on both strategic requirements and competing priorities within the imperial administration.

evidence.note: India's coastlines and trade required naval protection. Mixed crews and technical promotion offered institutional benefits, while administrative spending priorities constrained expansion.

segments.summary: The Indian naval case joins Indian Ocean security to the institutional value of a technically skilled, nationally mixed service.

segments.title: Indian railways and the immediate cost of development
segments.body: India's naval ambitions competed with the cost of improving its infrastructure. A single-track railway carrying vital goods and passengers left traffic vulnerable if that route failed. Doubling the track and providing alternative lines would improve resilience, but both required substantial investment. Taxes or borrowing by the British or Indian government would have to meet the immediate cost. The case for such spending rested on future prosperity and higher living standards, even when the eventual returns could not be predicted precisely.

evidence.note: Railway capacity and alternative routes required expensive investment, with immediate financing needs and benefits extending into future growth and living standards.

segments.summary: Railway resilience and naval expansion competed for investment that required immediate taxes or borrowing against uncertain future returns.

segments.title: French coalitions and fragmented shipbuilding
segments.body: French governments could change as parliamentary coalitions were rearranged without a new general election, repeatedly shifting ministerial priorities. The naval industry had a parallel coordination problem because individual yards altered common plans and produced ships that were difficult to operate as a uniform squadron. The yards could produce good vessels while still completing them slowly and introducing differences within a class. Combined with wartime demographic and psychological losses, those institutional problems complicated the prospect of a naval race with Italy.

evidence.note: Rapid turnover among French parliamentary coalitions repeatedly shifted naval priorities, while individual yards altered common plans and made uniform squadrons harder to produce. Wartime demographic and psychological losses made those coordination problems still more costly.

segments.summary: Rapid coalition turnover and independently minded yards made it harder for France to sustain coherent naval policy after the First World War.

segments.title: French disarmament required German weakness
segments.body: French leaders did not treat disarmament as a willingness to accept equal vulnerability. President Alexandre Millerand and Raymond Poincare wanted French armament to remain above Germany's, while the Treaty of Versailles suppressed German maritime industry and naval capacity. Britain also accepted that reduction of German sea power even when the allies differed elsewhere. The losses and psychological trauma of Verdun made security against Germany inseparable from the desire to prevent another war. France could therefore favour arms limitation while demanding an unequal postwar order.

evidence.note: Millerand and Poincare supported disarmament only while Germany remained weaker under Versailles restrictions, a security demand sharpened by the trauma of Verdun.

segments.summary: French support for disarmament remained conditional on Germany being kept weaker, while Verdun's trauma made another continental war intolerable.

segments.title: France, Italy, and the cost of naval parity
segments.body: France wanted to avoid an expensive naval race with Italy. Numerical parity nevertheless left different demands on the two fleets because France had commitments in Africa, the Caribbean, and the Far East. A French fleet matched to Italy had to choose between concentrating in the Mediterranean and protecting overseas possessions. Covering both would require Royal Navy support. The alternative proposed in this analysis was parity with Japan or an allowance above Italy's, but the Italian delegation would not accept a lower allowance than France.

evidence.note: France's overseas commitments complicated parity with Italy. The proposed alternatives were equality with Japan or a margin over Italy, which Italy would not accept.

segments.summary: French acceptance of parity with Italy created a mismatch between a Mediterranean fleet and France's wider colonial commitments.

segments.title: Sarraut, Jusserand, and France's fleet allowance
segments.body: Albert Sarraut's acceptance of parity with Italy rested, in this account, on an expectation that Italy would not maintain enough ships to make that equality a problem. Jules Jusserand raised the need for a larger French force. Once equality with Italy had been accepted as a condition, raising the shared allowance would leave that relationship unchanged. France's overseas commitments led to the proposed alternatives of parity with Japan or a margin above Italy. Italy's refusal to accept less than France constrained either approach.

evidence.note: Sarraut and Jusserand differed over the adequacy of French forces, while acceptance of parity with Italy constrained later bargaining over the ratio.

segments.summary: The French delegates' disagreement concerned both fleet requirements and what could still be negotiated after accepting equality with Italy.

segments.title: French naval support in British war planning
segments.body: British planning could treat French and Italian strength as cancelling each other in the Mediterranean. A Royal Navy reinforcement would then give France a margin over Italy, leaving Britain to cover the North Sea and send other forces to the Far East. This allocation depended on the French fleet continuing to contain Italy. The withdrawal of French naval support left Britain facing the Italian navy and uncertainty about the allegiance of French ships. Encounters with political figures at Washington and London also influenced later judgements of their reliability.

evidence.note: French-Italian balance supported British plans for limited Mediterranean reinforcement and concentration elsewhere. Loss of French support exposed that dependency, while earlier diplomatic contacts informed wartime assessments.

segments.summary: Plans to reinforce France against Italy helped Britain allocate ships elsewhere, making the loss of French support consequential for Mediterranean defence.

segments.title: Italian parity and Mediterranean concentration
segments.body: Ivanoe Bonomi and the Italian delegates sought equality in fleet allowance with France. Italy could focus on the Mediterranean while France had to account for overseas commitments as well. With Austria-Hungary broken up and neither Greece nor the Ottoman state posing the same naval challenge, France was Italy's principal regional rival short of the Royal Navy. The aspiration to make the sea Mare Nostrum predated Mussolini, although Bonomi still accounted for a continuing British presence. These circumstances explain the Italian delegation's insistence on an allowance equal to France's.

evidence.note: Italy's demand for parity with France reflected Mediterranean concentration, reduced regional rivals, and a Mare Nostrum aspiration that predated Mussolini.

segments.summary: Italy needed only parity with France to concentrate superior strength in the Mediterranean while France divided attention across an empire.

segments.title: Italian coalitions and opposition to Mussolini
segments.body: Italy's postwar coalitions combined factions whose electoral promises were difficult to fulfil together. Fear of the far left was one reason supporters rallied to Mussolini. Luigi Albertini, a delegate at Washington, later denounced Mussolini in parliament, sometimes to his face. In this interpretation, his continuing opposition illustrates the limits of Mussolini's attempt to establish a dictatorship compared with Nazi domination in Germany.

evidence.note: Disparate coalition commitments and fear of the far left accompany an interpretation of Mussolini's rise. Albertini's parliamentary opposition supplies the comparison with the extent of Nazi control in Germany.

segments.summary: Coalition instability and Albertini's parliamentary criticism provide context for a comparison of Fascist control in Italy and Nazi control in Germany.

segments.title: Japan's seven-to-ten risk-fleet logic
segments.body: Japan's desired seven-to-ten ratio was a deterrent calculation rather than a promise of outright victory. Japanese planners understood their industrial limits in a prolonged war against Britain or the United States, which helps explain their focus on short-war plans. Unlike Tirpitz's risk-fleet theory, this calculation did not depend on a third power exploiting the attacker's losses. Japan wanted an attack to cost enough that Britain or America would undertake it only with a strong reason. The fear was of suffering imperial intervention like that inflicted on China and other countries. The final 5:3 ratio largely preserved the existing balance, leaving Japan without the increase its leaders had sought.

evidence.note: The seven-to-ten demand sought deterrence against imperial intervention despite Japan's industrial limits. The accepted 5:3 ratio closely matched the existing balance.

segments.summary: Japan sought a seven-to-ten ratio to make intervention costly, despite recognising that it could not sustain a long war with Britain or the United States.

segments.title: Japanese diplomacy and trans-Pacific miscommunication
segments.body: British officials came somewhat closer to understanding Japanese diplomatic language because the alliance and long technical relationship had built more personal contact. American and French audiences had less shared context for Japanese illustrative phrasing. The later experience of Ambassador Masanao Hanihara, whose comments on American immigration legislation were read as a threat, demonstrates the danger. Translation skill mattered, but hostile listeners could also seize on ambiguity, allowing cultural and political suspicion to magnify disagreement.

evidence.note: Anglo-Japanese experience eased some diplomatic translation, while less shared context helped turn Hanihara's immigration statement into an apparent threat in the United States.

segments.summary: Different diplomatic idioms turned Japanese attempts at explanation into apparent threats and deepened an already suspicious American relationship.

segments.title: Equal ratios and unequal global commitments
segments.body: Italy obtained parity with France while remaining dissatisfied with the age of its ships. France's equal allowance had to serve more widely dispersed commitments. The treaty also matched Britain to a two-ocean United States even though the Royal Navy had major obligations in the Atlantic, Mediterranean, Indian Ocean, and Pacific. Capital ships could be concentrated for battle or dispersed to demonstrate commitment and deter conflict, but could not perform both tasks everywhere at once. Equal fleet totals therefore left different demands on the available ships, especially when peacetime presence required capital ships away from the main fleet.

evidence.note: Italy's parity came with dissatisfaction over old ships. Equal fleet allowances left France and Britain with different geographic commitments from Italy and the United States, alongside competing demands for capital-ship concentration and presence.

segments.summary: Formal Anglo-American equality concealed the Royal Navy's wider geographic obligations and the tension between battle concentration and peacetime presence.

segments.title: How naval limits could deepen later fear
segments.body: The treaty left several powers dissatisfied with the forces available for their commitments. In this interpretation, the constraints on naval strength helped create a perceived need for rearmament before Britain and France could confront new threats in 1938-39. The naval treaty system constrained fleets without similarly restricting armies and air forces, making naval rearmament different from expansion of the land and air services. Governments could delay intervention until they felt stronger at sea. Excessive armament could also increase fear, leaving a difficult balance between limits and confidence in national security.

evidence.note: Treaty constraints could weaken deterrent confidence, making later naval rearmament a precondition for intervention and thereby delaying action.

segments.summary: Naval disarmament could leave governments feeling too weak to intervene until they had rebuilt their fleets.

segments.title: Testing treaty arithmetic with an Australian capital ship
segments.body: An alternative treaty arrangement that allowed Australia to retain a capital ship is posed as an open counterfactual exercise. The questions concern the allowance needed, which ship Australia could keep, and how it would use that vessel. The premise is that Britain could not spare a capital ship for Australia while limited to 15 itself, so a larger total or different arrangement would be necessary. An Australian exception would raise further questions about a Canadian capital ship or an Indian cruiser squadron. The British programme envisaged 40-48 County-class cruisers, with roughly 18-23 intended for the Dominions. Those proposed numbers connect the exercise to the distribution of naval costs and forces within the empire; no final answer is supplied.

evidence.note: An unanswered counterfactual asks how Australia could retain a capital ship despite Britain's 15-ship limit, with implications for Canada, India, and the proposed County-class programme.

segments.summary: An Australian capital ship would require different treaty arithmetic and raise further questions about Canadian and Indian naval forces.
